title: Pick the best turn at every junction
allegory: Policy improvement is rerouting with a scored map: at every junction, add the reward on each road to the old plan's score for where that road lands, and take the best one; a plan built this way is never worse anywhere.
map: the roads out of a junction
the old plan's score pinned on every junction
V_π, the value of each state under the current policy
reward on the road plus the score of where it lands
taking the best-scoring road at every junction
π'(s) = argmaxₐ Q_π(s, a), guaranteed V_π' ≥ V_π everywhere

cap.1: You have a plan and a score for every square: how good it is to stand there if you follow the plan. Now use those scores to make a better plan.
cap.2: Policy evaluation gave you V_π, the value of each state under a fixed policy π. Policy improvement turns those numbers into a new policy that is at least as good.
cap.3: Given V_π for a deterministic policy on a known MDP (T and R handed to you as arrays), construct π' with V_π' ≥ V_π in every state.

cap.1: At a junction, for each road add the reward on it to the score of where it lands. Take the road with the biggest total. Do this at every junction.
cap.2: For each state, score each action by expected reward plus γ times the old value of where it leads. The new policy takes the best-scoring action everywhere.
cap.3: π'(s) = argmaxₐ Σ_{s'} T(s'|s,a)(R(s,a,s') + γV_π(s')) = argmaxₐ Q_π(s,a): greedy with respect to the old policy's own action values.

parts.note: old score of where it lands

cap.1: One line: at every square, pick the move with the best reward-plus-future. The future is priced with the old plan's scores, not the new plan's.
cap.2: In code: build a (states × actions) table of one-step values from T, R and V, then take argmax over actions. That is policy_improvement.
cap.3: Q = Σ_{s'} T[s,a,s'](R[s,a,s'] + γV[s']) as one einsum, then π' = Q.argmax(-1). V comes from π, so this is a one-step lookahead, not a full re-plan.

chapters.name: Never worse
chapters.title: V before and after one greedy pass (corridor, γ = 0.9)

cap.1: A tiny corridor with the goal on the right. The old plan shuffled back and forth in the middle. One greedy pass later, every square's score rose or stayed put.
cap.2: Old policy: s0 → right, s1 → left (a loop), s2 → right, so V = [0, 0, 1]. Greedy on V picks right everywhere: V' = [0.81, 0.9, 1].
cap.3: Policy improvement theorem: greedy w.r.t. V_π gives V_π' ≥ V_π pointwise. Deterministic policies are finite, so alternating evaluate and improve terminates at an optimum.

chapters.name: The flip-flop

left.title: ties go to the first action

chapters.verdict: Two optimal plans can take turns forever. Break ties the same way every time.

cap.1: If two roads score exactly the same and you pick between them at random, the plan keeps changing without getting better, so 'nothing changed' never happens.
cap.2: find_optimal_policy stops when the policy array is unchanged. Break ties differently each call and two equally good policies swap forever. np.argmax always takes the first maximum.
cap.3: Ties in Q_π make the greedy policy non-unique; inconsistent tie-breaking gives a 2-cycle between optimal policies. Compare with (pi_new == pi_old).all(), and keep γ < 1.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Evaluate, then improve: every RL loop
Q-learning and DQN act greedily on estimates
Greedy on a flawed score exploits its flaws

cap.1: Score the plan, improve it, repeat. Nearly every way of training an agent, including the ones used to shape chatbots, is this loop with the map taken away.
cap.2: SARSA, Q-learning and DQN run this loop from samples instead of known T and R. Acting greedily on estimated values is where exploration and over-optimisation troubles start.
cap.3: The guarantee assumes exact V_π. Greedy improvement against learned values or rewards also exploits their errors, one reason RLHF keeps a KL penalty to a reference policy.

caption.1: Slide the discount up and watch the best road change from quick reward (A) to patient payoff (C). At exactly 0.50, A and B tie. Then add ice to road C.
caption.2: Each bar is reward + γ × value of where the road lands: the one-step lookahead. Ice lowers C's expected landing value, and the greedy pick falls back to B or A.
caption.3: With p = 0 the argmax switches at γ = 0.5 (A to B) and γ = 2/3 (B to C). The slip chance scales C's future term by (1 − p): an expectation over T.

hamming.what: Build a new plan by taking, in every state, the action with the best one-step lookahead under the current plan's values.
hamming.when: Right after evaluating a policy, as the second half of policy iteration, and implicitly whenever an agent acts greedily on its value estimates.
hamming.why: It is guaranteed never to make things worse, so alternating it with evaluation climbs to an optimal policy in a finite number of rounds.

object.title: The rising gridworld
object.subtitle: A 4 × 4 world with the goal in the top-right corner; each square's pillar is its value after each round of evaluate-then-improve.

cap.1: A 4 × 4 world with the goal in the top-right corner. The first plan, always go left, never gets there, so every square scores 0.
cap.2: Round 0: V of the all-left policy is 0 everywhere. The goal square is terminal, so its pillar stays flat.
cap.3: γ = 0.9, deterministic moves, +1 only on entering the goal; V_π0 ≡ 0 and greedy ties break to the first action (up).

cap.1: One greedy pass. Squares beside the goal step into it, ties elsewhere happen to point up, and the two columns nearest the goal light up.
cap.2: Round 1: exact evaluation of the new plan credits every square whose chosen move chains to the goal: 1, 0.9, 0.81, 0.729.
cap.3: V_π1 ≥ V_π0 pointwise; each value is γ^(steps − 1) along the chain the new policy follows.

cap.1: Another pass: the good news spreads one column further left. No square ever loses score.
cap.2: Round 2: column 1 fills in. Every pillar rose or stayed put: the improvement theorem in action.
cap.3: Monotone improvement V_π2 ≥ V_π1; value information propagates outward from the terminal reward.

cap.1: Round 3: every square has its best score. One more pass only swaps between equally good moves; after that nothing changes and the loop stops.
cap.2: Round 3 is optimal, V = γ^(steps − 1). A further pass just swaps tied actions, which is why deterministic tie-breaking lets the loop terminate.
cap.3: Three improvements reach V*; the next greedy step changes only tied actions (same V), and the one after leaves the policy array unchanged.

predict.q: You act greedily with respect to your current plan's own values. Can the new plan be worse anywhere?

options.t: No: never worse in any state
Yes: it may trade some states for others

predict.why: The policy improvement theorem: greedy w.r.t. V_π gives V_π' ≥ V_π in every state.

predict.q: Two actions tie for best and you choose randomly each round. What can happen?

options.t: The policy flips forever and the loop never stops

predict.why: Both policies are optimal, but the 'policy unchanged' check never fires. Break ties deterministically, e.g. with np.argmax.

predict.q: Why is the future priced with the old plan's values, not the new plan's?

options.t: V_π is all you have; the new plan gets scored next round
Old values are always more accurate

predict.why: Improvement is a one-step lookahead on V_π. Evaluating the new policy is the next half of policy iteration.

object.where: Any 'good news spreads backwards from the goal' process: route planning, chess endgame tables, dynamic programming.
